original_question: Which gene is known to have mutations that cause Albers-Schönberg disease (autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II)?

final_qi.question: Which gene is known to have mutations that cause Albers-Schönberg disease (autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II)?
final_qi.long_answer: Albers-Schönberg disease, the classical form of autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II, is produced by heterozygous mutations in the CLCN7 gene. CLCN7 encodes the chloride channel 7 (ClC-7) that partners with the V-ATPase in osteoclast ruffled borders to exchange chloride ions for protons. Pathogenic CLCN7 variants impair acidification of the resorption lacuna, preventing normal bone matrix dissolution and leading to the increased bone density characteristic of ADO2.

final_answer.long_answer: Albers-Schönberg disease, also called autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II, is classically caused by heterozygous mutations in the CLCN7 gene. CLCN7 encodes the chloride channel 7 that partners with the V-ATPase in osteoclasts to acidify the resorption lacuna. Dominant-negative or loss-of-function mutations in CLCN7 impair this acidification, preventing normal bone resorption and leading to the dense, brittle bones characteristic of Albers-Schönberg disease.
